questions.question: Define a galaxy and name the force that holds it together. Describe what Galileo discovered about the Milky Way, and explain what the dark lanes in the Milky Way are.
questions.expected_answer: A galaxy is an enormous collection of stars, gas, dust and dark matter held together by gravity. In 1610 Galileo looked at the Milky Way through a telescope and found that its glow is made of a vast number of faint stars, too dim and close together to be seen separately with the naked eye. The dark lanes are clouds of dust in the disc that block the light of the stars behind them (for example the Coalsack near the Southern Cross); they are not empty gaps.

questions.question: Describe the shape and size of the Milky Way. Name its main parts and state what lies at its centre.
questions.expected_answer: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy: a central bulge stretched into a bar, surrounded by a thin flat disc with curved spiral arms of stars, gas and dust, all inside a roughly spherical halo of old stars, globular clusters and dark matter. The disc is about 100 000 light years across but only about 1 000 light years thick. It contains about 100 to 400 billion stars. The spiral arms are bright because they contain young, hot stars and glowing gas where new stars form. At the centre is a supermassive black hole, Sagittarius A*, of about four million solar masses.

questions.question: Describe the Sun's position in the Milky Way and explain why we see the galaxy as a band of light across the sky. State how the Sun moves within the galaxy.
questions.expected_answer: The Sun lies in the disc, about 26 000 light years from the centre (roughly halfway to the edge), near the Orion Arm. Because we are inside the flat disc, looking along the disc in any direction we see huge numbers of distant stars stacked up, which appear as a band circling the sky; looking out of the disc we see far fewer stars. The centre lies towards Sagittarius and Scorpius, high over South Africa on winter evenings, so the band is brightest then. Gravity pulls the Sun towards the galactic centre while its sideways speed (about 230 km/s) keeps it in orbit; one orbit (a galactic year) takes about 230 million years.
